summary.title: Medieval bearer register, c.1175–1500
summary.wikitreeId: Space:Bearers of the ''de Glasgu'' Name and the Emergence of the Glasgow Surname, c.1175–1500
summary.provenance: Reviewed Glasgow Name Study synthesis, 7 September 2026; individual bearer source copies verified live 29 August 2026.
summary.confidence: Mixed: individual occurrences are documented; a continuous medieval pedigree is not.
summary.conclusion: The records document personal de Glasgu/de Glascu usage from the late twelfth century and two explicit father–son statements. They do not join the named bearers into one family or prove hereditary surname use in every occurrence.
summary.completedSearches: Guild-roll, cartulary, ecclesiastical, royal-account and charter references were compared; distinct same-name people were kept separate and fourteen verified individual bearer pages were recorded locally.
summary.nextAction: Add only a record with an identifying bridge—kin term, office, property, patron or repeated associates—before proposing any new connection.
summary.localStatus: Full public-safe local edition published; WikiTree comparison and outgoing draft available on the reading page.

summary.title: Early Irish branches and Ulster locality groups
summary.provenance: Maintained early-Ireland synthesis; Betham GO MS 225 p. 90/image 97 and new PRONI Lifford catalogue transcriptions inspected 30 September 2026.
summary.confidence: Direct Archibald–Thomas father clause in Betham; son-to-Lifford identity strongly probable; wider regional and Scottish bridges unresolved.
summary.conclusion: Betham’s April 1673 will abstract identifies Archibald of Rathmalton’s eldest son Thomas and only daughter Margaret. Matching the son to the Lifford/Raphoe man remains strongly probable and his father field uncertain. Other Ulster household networks remain separate; no single Irish founder or Scottish descent is established.
summary.completedSearches: Religious returns, leases, parish material, wills, census households, land records, family papers and relevant Y-DNA context were compared in the reviewed Name Study.
summary.nextAction: Seek a distinctive relative or estate connecting the named 1673 son to Thomas of Lifford; search NAI PRCT/1/1 microfilm MFGS/41/1, deed recitals and Cairns/M’Auley collateral records. The surviving book is now accessible; its G index and Glas* transcript search did not locate the particular will. A complete manual search remains unfinished.

summary.title: Scottish branches, c.1447–1650
summary.wikitreeId: Space:Glasgow Branches in 15th and 16th Century Scotland
summary.provenance: Reviewed Glasgow Name Study synthesis, 7 September 2026. NRS B66/25/43 civic-status detail inspected 15 October 2026. Fisherrow printed-index pages inspected 15 October 2026. Carnwath printed passages and date schedule visually checked 15 October 2026. Mid Calder original and Maidment pp.395–396,399 visually reread/checked 15 October 2026; NLS court-book and transcript references located.
summary.confidence: High for the documented William–John burgh core; probable for several adjacent relationships; unproved between regional groups.
summary.conclusion: A Glasgow burgh family is directly visible through William Glasgow, Esbell Brade and their son John in sixteenth-century property records. A focused 1600–1650 Findmypast follow-up adds dated indexed records and qualified Fisherrow, Haddington and Irish leads, while original-page access limits and competing indexes remain explicit. The Saltmarket predecessor and several sibling links are probable, while the Corsinkell and Calder connections remain separate questions. The 8 August 1475 Stirling description groups John Glesgw among burgesses; one man across Glasgow 1447–1455 and Stirling 1475–1480 remains viable alongside close-family alternatives. Placeholder birth estimates do not choose the generations. The Fisherrow index gives James, son Alexander and Edward the same 1624 date, volume and folio; identification with Edward-1557 is a possible bridge to his tentative Corsankell line, with exact kinship open. Later checked columns repeatedly associate Alexander with James the weaver in 1646–1647; Edward shares the first 1646 reference. Exact identities remain open. Eduard-994, indexed in 1609 with father James, is an alternative Edward identity that may place the association within the proposed Fisherrow household. John and Thomas are documented at Quothquan in the 1520s; John is at Upper Quothquan in 1531/32. They form a possible predecessor group for the later weaver James, with no intervening generations yet established. The original Mid Calder baptism of 17 February 1605 names father James Glasgow, provisionally in Muirestoun, and adult witness George Glasgow. The 1586 Calder muster list names George Glasgw in Mureistoun. Murieston is the probable common locality; the two older George occurrences may be one man, but no kinship is stated. The local working pedigree now selects four uncertain father links: Andrew3163 to James991, John1561 and David1028; John3296 to John3610. They are logical hypotheses from the existing accounts, with no shared mother or confident upgrade. Three further low-confidence working placements choose William-1098 for Michael-3911, Andrew-3163 for Jonat-3262, and Ninian-3188 for Barbara-3182. Exact collateral degrees and identity alternatives remain open.
summary.completedSearches: Property, burgess, protocol, testament and regional-record evidence was reconciled in the reviewed Name Study; conflicting kin claims were separated from explicit parent-child statements. The third Stirling occurrence is integrated at archive-description level; the original charter remains to inspect.
summary.nextAction: Begin with original witness wording, title recitals and endorsements linking the 1447–1480 John record groups; then seek the Saltmarket John-to-William transfer of 1527–1528/29. Retain the 1506 alias-Smith identification as possible, and extend supported sibling links without inventing intervening parents. For Fisherrow, read RS25 9/135 and 10/171 for Edward’s role and named kin. For the Campbeltown outlier, compare the original 1659 household with the 1605, 1622 and 1627 George baptisms; no candidate is selected. Read RS25 33/258, 33/360 and 34/287 for kin and title continuity; do not conflate James the weaver with the earlier tailor.

summary.title: County Londonderry families
summary.provenance: Local revision draft marked REVIEW; canonical WikiTree page captured 29 August 2026 (last listed WikiTree edit 21 July 2026).
summary.confidence: Partial: the Tamlaght O'Crilly–Inishrush people form a documentary locality study; the proposed wider relationship is unproved.
summary.conclusion: The maintained dossier distinguishes Hugh, Adam and John Glasgow evidence in Tamlaght O'Crilly and Inishrush from a single-founder narrative. It supports a research group, not a proved county-wide pedigree.
summary.completedSearches: The local dossier compares the 1740 return, Inishrush lease context, later locality references and the reconstructed nineteenth-century John household.
summary.nextAction: Compare the REVIEW-marked local revision against the existing canonical page, then seek records that expressly connect the separate households before naming a common ancestor.
